newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blasts Colombia's prison terms for drug lords.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blasts Colombia's prison terms for drug lords.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday the luxurious prison conditions and lenient sentencing enjoyed by Colombian drug kingpins would be factors in determining if Colombia would be "certified" a U.S. ally in the war on drug trafficking.

"They're called jails but they're more like penthouses," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters. "They don't have a cement bed. They have, you know, all of the trappings of a multimillionaire drug kingpin life. They live the high life in jail."

Burns also criticised the sentences handed down on Friday by a Colombian judge against Cali drug cartel leaders Miguel and Gilberto Rodriguez Orejuela, who may spend as little as five years in jail for their crimes.

The billionaire Rodriguez brothers were sentenced to 18 and 21 years in prison for crimes like drug smuggling and possession of illegal weapons, but their prison terms were halved under Colombia's plea bargaining programme.
The pair, who masterminded the world's most powerful cocaine-running network, may go free even sooner for good behaviour and for studying while in prison.

Burns said Colombia's sentencing system and its prison conditions would be considered in the upcoming round of "certification," Washington's annual evaluation of how other governments fight against drugs.
In March 1996 the United States "decertified" Colombia, charging it had allowed the cartels to corrupt every level of its government.
Countries placed on that blacklist, such as Afghanistan, Burma and Nigeria, face U.S. economic sanctions.
However, Burns made a rare favourable comment about Colombian President Ernesto Samper, who last year lost his U.S. tourist visa due to his alleged ties with the cartels.
"...we've been very pleased to see even the Colombian president, President Samper, question the Colombian judicial system, a system that offers these light sentences," he said.

The United States believes that Samper took some $6 million from the Cali cartel to finance his 1994 presidential campaign. Colombia's Congress dismissed similar charges against the president in 1996.
